item.title: SageMaker HyperPod Adds Cluster Extensions and Global Inference Gateway
item.description:
SageMaker HyperPod Adds Cluster Extensions and Global Inference Gateway

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod has introduced two new capabilities: cluster extensions for managing software on running nodes and the Global Inference Gateway for routing requests across multiple clusters and regions. These updates aim to reduce configuration drift and simplify the management of distributed AI inference workloads.

🧩 Cluster Extensions for Node Consistency

Managing a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development involves keeping configuration, software, network topology, and user rosters in sync with the actual nodes. Over time, these elements drift apart, and there is no automated way to detect when they do.

In November 2026, AWS launched cluster extensions to address the software and settings on running nodes. These are software packages managed by AWS that administrators can install, configure, update, and remove through APIs or the Amazon SageMaker AI console.

Key features of cluster extensions include:

  • Managed Extensions: Initial support includes observability and user management (including directory integration).
  • Automatic Application: HyperPod applies extensions to every node, including those added via scale-up or replacement, maintaining consistency as the cluster scales and heals.
  • Simplified Updates: Settings can be changed or versions upgraded via API calls or the console, eliminating the need to edit scripts and replace nodes.
  • Visibility: Each extension reports its status and per-node health.

Administrators should use cluster extensions for managed software capabilities. Custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts remain the correct approach for organization-specific software or initialization not covered by available extensions.

🌐 Global Inference Gateway

Previously, the SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway provided a single, GPU-aware endpoint for individual clusters. However, during traffic peaks, requests could queue on a saturated cluster while GPUs on another cluster, potentially in a different AWS Region, sat idle. Managing this required building and maintaining load balancers, DNS, and cross-Region networking manually.

The Global Inference Gateway is a SageMaker-managed gateway that routes across every registered cluster, whether in a single Region or across multiple Regions.

How it works:

  • Routing: The gateway picks the best cluster and carries the request over the AWS backbone.
  • Failover: If a cluster fails, the gateway moves traffic to the next-best cluster automatically.
  • Endpoint Consolidation: Clients call a single SageMaker-managed endpoint instead of tracking one endpoint per cluster or model.
  • Security: Every request is authenticated with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and IAM, and reaches clusters only over AWS PrivateLink.

For example, a team serving four models across five HyperPod clusters in two Regions would normally track 20 endpoints (one per model per cluster). The Inference Gateway cuts this to five, and the Global Inference Gateway consolidates further by handling cross-region overflow during peaks.

⚙️ Integration with Existing HyperPod Features

The Global Inference Gateway is the second tier of the architecture described in the initial Inference Gateway launch. It integrates with existing HyperPod infrastructure:

  • Configuration: Administrators enable global routing by turning on the spec.globalRouting block in the cluster’s existing InferenceGatewayConfig.
  • Creation: The CreateGlobalInferenceGateway API call registers clusters to route across, and SageMaker returns one endpoint.
  • Publishing: The HyperPod Inference controller publishes the cluster privately from the user’s account, creating a Network Load Balancer, publishing a VPC endpoint service, and uploading the listener’s certificate to the user’s TLS bucket.
  • Request Flow: Clients sign requests with SigV4 and send them to the gateway’s regional endpoint. The gateway authenticates the caller, selects the best cluster, and uses AWS PrivateLink to carry the request to that cluster, where the local Inference Gateway routes it to the appropriate model pod.

💡 Why It Matters

These developments address two major pain points in large-scale AI infrastructure. First, they eliminate the “drift” between desired cluster state and actual node software by using managed extensions that automatically apply to new nodes. Second, they solve the inefficiency of idle GPUs during regional traffic peaks by enabling global routing that balances load across regions without manual load balancer management. For users like Bagelcode, who run LLM inference services on AWS, the Global Inference Gateway allows serving models across multiple regions through a single endpoint while maintaining high availability.

#SageMaker #HyperPod #Slurm #AWS #Inference #MachineLearning

Source: Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm | Amazon Web Services Source: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Kronk Released as a Go SDK and Server for Local AI Inference
item.description:
Kronk Released as a Go SDK and Server for Local AI Inference

Kronk has been released as a Go SDK and production-ready model server designed for hardware-accelerated local inference. It allows developers to use Go to directly integrate llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, and stable-diffusion.cpp into their applications.

🔍 Overview

The Kronk model server is built on the same public SDKs that are available to Go applications. The system provides a high-level API and integrates with OpenWebUI, OpenCode, and Claude Code. It also includes features for model management, security, observability, and a browser interface.

⚙️ Key Components

The capabilities of Kronk are divided across several subsystems and SDK features:

Subsystem / Component Supported Capabilities and Features
Kronk SDK Text generation, streaming, reasoning, tool calls, vision, embeddings, reranking, typed Decision questions, buffered text-to-speech, concurrent processing, and incremental message caching.
Kronk Model Server OpenAI-compatible APIs (for Chat Completions, Responses, embeddings, reranking, and audio transcription), Anthropic-compatible Messages API, and Decision endpoints at /v1/systemone and /v1/decide.
Speech Supports Chatterbox Turbo and Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base with memory planning and typed pools across native backends. Currently SDK-only (no HTTP speech-generation endpoint or BUI speech playground).
Bucky File transcription, translation, channel-separated diarization, and live streaming transcription.
Experimental Malina Text-to-image, image-to-image, Canny ControlNet conditioning, ADetailer face refinement, AnimateDiff video generation, Real-ESRGAN upscaling, single-checkpoint and multi-file diffusion pipelines, and Motion-JPEG encoding. Currently SDK-only.

🧩 Hardware Acceleration and Dependencies

Kronk’s performance and execution model rely on several hardware and library management behaviors:

  • Automatic Downloads: The first model or SDK example that runs can download the compatible native libraries and model files automatically.
  • Library Management: Every Kronk release is bound to known-compatible library versions. Instead of mixing native libraries from unrelated releases, users should use each subsystem’s downloader. Upstream changes can require coordinated releases of Yzma, Bucky, Malina, and Kronk.
  • Acceleration Support: Hardware acceleration depends on the operating system, architecture, inference engine, and library bundle. Not every backend is available for every SDK or architecture, and non-Metal memory estimates are provisional.
  • Formula Trust: The fully qualified formula name trusts only the Kronk formula, rather than every item in the ardanlabs/kronk tap.

#Golang #Inference #LLM #DeveloperTools

Source: ardanlabs/kronk

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing

Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports to send each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy.

🔍 Overview

KV-aware routing is designed for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. It addresses limitations in the previously introduced prefix-aware routing, which infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone. Because prefix-aware routing hashes the start of the request, it cannot tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Consequently, if an instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. Additionally, in multi-turn chats, each turn adds to the history; while a request is shorter than the configured PrefixLength, every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns.

🧩 How it works

A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. KV-aware routing operates through three main components:

  • Model Container Reporting: The model container reports what it has cached.
  • Managed Cache Index: SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint.
  • Endpoint Routing: The endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request.

When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. If instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A.

The endpoint picks among candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing.

⚙️ Key details

You turn on KV-aware routing in two places:

  • Add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents.
  • Set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration.

Specifically, when you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG, the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. Clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. You do not configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing.

💡 Why it matters

This strategy ensures that requests sharing a prompt are routed to instances where that prompt is already in the GPU memory cache, maximizing computational efficiency. By tracking actual cache eviction and storage events rather than relying on static prefix hashes, the system prevents routing requests to instances where the cache has been cleared due to memory pressure.

#AmazonSageMaker #LLM #KVCache #Routing #Inference

Source: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing | Amazon Web Services

item.title: SageMaker HyperPod Inference Adds NVIDIA Dynamo Support for Distributed AI
item.description:
SageMaker HyperPod Inference Adds NVIDIA Dynamo Support for Distributed AI

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo, combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address challenges such as GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights exceeding the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead.

🧩 How it works

Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery.

The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components:

  • HyperPod Inference Operator: Manages endpoint deployment through an InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) custom resource, using its dynamoSpec section to supply the Dynamo configuration.
  • Dynamo Operator: Manages resources defined in a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD), including the frontend, model workers, replica counts, and resource requirements.
  • Grove: Coordinates related groups of pods, including multi-node workers, and their scaling relationships.
  • Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler: Places pods on GPU resources, using gang scheduling to schedule the pods required for a multi-node worker together.
  • AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs): Provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions.

The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA. Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies; prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers.

⚙️ Key details

  • Deployment Paths: Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec support invocation through SageMaker endpoints. Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment.
  • Inference Engines: You can choose vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, with vLLM used by default. The operator also supplies defaults for KV-aware routing and replica counts.
  • Configuration: Both paths support single-instance and multi-node deployments. Dynamo-specific settings belong under spec.dynamoSpec. For example, a configuration might run one model-worker replica across two instances (16 GPUs) with two frontend replicas for request handling. Setting dynamoSpec.frontend.routingMode to kv-aware turns on KV-aware routing.
  • Health Management: HyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers.

💡 Why it matters

For teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data. Splunk, a Cisco company, faced exactly this when building evaluation models for its Agent Observability product. “For Splunk Agent Observability, our ability to train robust GenAI Eval models relies on access to high-quality, diverse datasets which are hard to curate for very specific tasks. Amazon SageMaker AI data preparation capabilities for synthetic data generation is meaningfully helping us scale these capabilities. We’ve been able to generate statistically representative synthetic datasets reliably and fast, while preserving the underlying patterns our models depend on. The seamless integration with the rest of our SageMaker workflow means our data scientists and customers spend less time wrangling data and more time building models that drive real enterprise value through Splunk.” — Yash Sheth, Director of Engineering, Splunk Agent Observability

Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block that you can use on its own or chain together.

  • Auto-labeling: Label data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all. Built-in task types include classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, and you can define custom tasks. For tasks with a fixed set of possible answers, a jury of several models labels each row, and their level of agreement becomes that row’s confidence score.
  • Human Review: Rows below your confidence threshold go to a review queue in Amazon SageMaker Studio, which uses the open-source Label Studio Community Edition. Reviewer corrections feed back into auto-labeling, and you can generate consensus metrics and labeling reports.
  • Synthetic Data Generation: Generate training, evaluation, and test data from a specification. You can ground the output in your own seed data and documents, and the service generates a code-based data generation pipeline that you can review, modify, reuse, and scale.
  • Data Quality Evaluation: Check datasets against your own business rules, built-in metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics. Find duplicates and near-duplicates, and surface issues you didn’t think to check for, such as label noise or answer leakage.
  • Data Transformation: Clean and reshape data for your target training technique. Describe the change in plain language and have the code generated for you, use built-in operations such as dedupe, merge, split, and filter, or run your own Python at scale.

#SageMaker #NVIDIA #Dynamo #Inference #DataPreparation

Source: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference | Amazon Web Services Source: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Stable Sampling and Head-Specific Fixes Improve Long-Form AI Performance
item.description:
Stable Sampling and Head-Specific Fixes Improve Long-Form AI Performance

Recent findings indicate that the performance of open-weight language models during long generation depends heavily on the sampling method used, while specific attention heads in sparse models often cause long-context retrieval failures.

🔍 Overview

  • Open-weight models frequently degrade in quality as generation length increases.
  • Standard attempts to fix this often involve additional training.
  • At high temperature, the sampler— the rule selecting the next token— determines whether long and agentic generation succeeds.
  • Sparse attention models that read limited key blocks can lose significant long-context retrieval accuracy.

🧩 How it works

Sampling Stability

  • Top-nsigma: Keeps the pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises, maintaining accuracy without letting in low-probability tokens.
  • Top-p / Top-k: Pool sizes grow significantly with temperature. For example, in Llama-3.1-8B, top-p’s pool grew from 4 tokens at temperature 1 to 51,845 at temperature 2.
  • Mechanism: Counting how many tokens a sampler lets through explains performance differences. Top-nsigma stops collapsing when the pool is picked at temperature 1 and temperature is applied afterwards.

Attention Head Calibration

  • Diagnosis: A calibration probe identifies “blind” attention heads that miss the needle in retrieval tasks.
  • Metrics: The probe reads two quantities in every head: the forfeited needle attention and the share of the answer’s log-probability restored by fixing the selection.
  • Root Cause: These heads attend to the needle, but a mean-pooled key summary dilutes the single decisive token.
  • Solution: Applying full attention in specific identified heads or using a 4-bit scorer recovers accuracy without retraining the model.

⚙️ Key details

Benchmark / Model Condition Result
Qwen3.5 (Coding Agents) Temp 2, top-p/top-k/Top-H 0/100 GitHub issues resolved
Qwen3.5 (Coding Agents) Temp 2, top-nsigma 46 to 62 issues resolved
All Benchmarks (Median) Top-nsigma vs Top-p 100% vs 26% of temp-1 score retained
MiniCPM4.1-8B (64K) Multi-key Retrieval Accuracy increased from 54.1% to 97.5%
Qwen3-8B (SeerAttention-R) Multi-key Retrieval Accuracy increased from 29.8% to 97.7%
  • Correlation: Typical pool size predicts judged quality with a Spearman correlation of -0.77 across 133 sampler/temperature combinations.
  • Latency Trade-off: In production serving, full attention in fixed heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) saved by sparse attention at 32K to 128K contexts.
  • Model Consistency: Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads.

💡 Why it matters

  • Top-nsigma and similar stable samplers prevent the degradation seen in long-form writing, structured outputs, and coding agents at high temperatures.
  • Identifying and fixing specific attention heads allows sparse attention models to achieve near-full attention retrieval accuracy while maintaining high inference speeds.
  • The findings suggest that sampler behavior and targeted attention head modifications are more effective for long-context stability than additional training.

🚀 Availability

  • All code and data related to the sampler tests are released to the public.

#LargeLanguageModels #Inference #AttentionMechanism #OpenWeights #LongContext

Source: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat) Source: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention

item.title: LLMKube Unifies LLM Inference Across GPU Fleets
item.description:
LLMKube Unifies LLM Inference Across GPU Fleets

LLMKube is a Kubernetes operator that manages LLM inference across heterogeneous GPU fleets, including NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple Silicon hosts. It turns deployment into a two-resource YAML setup and can expose models through an OpenAI-compatible API.

🔍 Overview

Define a Model and an InferenceService; the operator handles model downloading and caching, GPU scheduling, health checks, scaling, and API exposure. Linux GPU pods and Apple Silicon hosts both appear as InferenceService objects to kubectl.

🧩 How it works

The system has two cooperating processes:

  • An in-cluster controller manages Kubernetes-side desired state.
  • An optional out-of-cluster metal-agent is used for Apple Silicon hosts. It supervises OS-level processes and registers authenticated ingress with the cluster. An in-cluster relay fronts that ingress, so Metal InferenceService objects are ordinary Services.

On Apple Silicon, inference runs as native macOS processes rather than containers, allowing full Metal GPU access.

⚙️ Supported hardware and runtimes

Hardware or runtime Details in the evidence
NVIDIA CUDA support
AMD Vulkan support
Intel Listed among supported heterogeneous fleet hosts
Apple Silicon Metal support; native macOS inference processes
Runtimes llama.cpp, vLLM, TGI, and mlx-server
Apple Silicon processes The Metal Agent runs llama-server, mlx-server, and vllm-swift

Other capabilities include multi-GPU sharding, model caching, and running models across NVIDIA, Apple Silicon, and AMD from one spec.

🔐 Routing and policy

Adding a ModelRouter enables policy-aware routing between local models and external providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and LiteLLM. A rule matching requests labeled pii/phi by header can route only to local-tier backends. Content detection is planned (#441).

🚀 Availability and maturity

LLMKube is Apache-2.0 licensed, actively developed, and intended to run across homelab and on-prem fleets. It is pre-1.0: every CRD is v1alpha1, and fields can change between minor releases. For running one model on one laptop, Ollama is simpler.

#Kubernetes #LLM #Inference #GPUs #OpenAIAPI

Source: defilantech/LLMKube

item.title: NVIDIA launches Dynamo as open-source datacenter-scale inference orchestration layer
item.description:
NVIDIA launches Dynamo as open-source datacenter-scale inference orchestration layer

NVIDIA has announced Dynamo, an open-source, datacenter-scale inference stack built in Rust and Python that serves as an orchestration layer above existing inference engines. Dynamo does not replace SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, or vLLM; instead, it turns them into a coordinated multi-node inference system.

🧩 How it works

Dynamo integrates several key capabilities to optimize performance across diverse workloads:

  • Disaggregated serving for efficient resource allocation
  • Intelligent routing to direct requests optimally
  • Multi-tier KV caching to reduce latency
  • Automatic scaling to adapt to workload demand

These features work together to maximize throughput and minimize latency for LLM, reasoning, multimodal, and video generation workloads.

⚙️ Key details

The platform is designed for extensibility and performance:

  • Core language stack: Rust for performance, Python for extensibility
  • Open-source under Apache-2.0 license
  • Community-focused with 160+ contributors
  • Active SIG meetings including SIG Router and SIG Frontend (biweekly sync)

🚀 Availability

Dynamo is freely available through multiple channels:

  • GitHub repository: ai-dynamo/dynamo with latest releases
  • PyPI package: ai-dynamo
  • Documentation: NVIDIA Dynamo docs
  • Community Slack workspace: Join ai-dynamo workspace
  • DeepWiki: Ask DeepWiki

💡 Why it matters

Dynamo addresses the growing complexity of AI inference by providing a unified coordination layer that enables organizations to deploy and scale large language model workloads efficiently across distributed infrastructure, while preserving compatibility with existing inference engine investments.

#NVIDIA #AI #inference #Dynamo #LLM #open-source

Source: ai-dynamo/dynamo

item.title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin Achieves 10× Agentic Throughput Per Kilowatt in MLPerf Endpoints v1.0
item.description:
NVIDIA Vera Rubin Achieves 10× Agentic Throughput Per Kilowatt in MLPerf Endpoints v1.0

NVIDIA released provisional results for its Vera Rubin NVL72 platform in the MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 benchmark, showing more than 10× the agentic throughput per kilowatt compared to the verified GB300 NVL72 while maintaining a minimum end‑to‑end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user.

🔍 Overview

  • Agentic workloads are demanding more from inference systems.
  • AI agents carry growing conversation histories across turns and generate a mix of reasoning, tool calls, and responses.
  • Inference systems must support users at scale while remaining responsive.
  • The MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 dataset captures coding trajectories that accumulate history over many turns and enterprise workflows that reuse shared instructions, tool definitions, and business rules.

🧩 How It Works

  • The benchmark evaluates serving capacity and responsiveness using coding and enterprise workflows through API endpoints.
  • During performance runs, generated tool calls and workflow intent are checked against reference values.
  • Separate SWE‑bench Verified evaluations assess end‑to‑end task‑solving capability.
  • These checks evaluate whether faster serving preserves model quality.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Vera Rubin NVL72 (32 accelerators)
    • Run 9: concurrency = 1,024 queries
    • TTFT P90 = 4,673.9 ms
    • System TPS = 41,414.2 tokens/sec
    • E2E average interactivity = 50.4 tokens/sec per user
    • Operating power = 100.89 kW
  • GB300 NVL72 (48 accelerators)
    • Run 6: concurrency = 48 queries
    • TTFT P90 = 2,305.1 ms
    • System TPS = 2,210.4 tokens/sec
    • E2E average interactivity = 56.2 tokens/sec per user
    • Operating power = 60 kW

📊 Performance Results for Model Variants

  • Kimi K3
    • Vera Rubin: run 9, 1,024 queries, 41,414.2 TPS, 50.4 interactivity, 100.89 kW
    • GB300: run 6, 48 queries, 2,210.4 TPS, 56.2 interactivity, 60 kW
  • DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash
    • Vera Rubin: run 6, 1,408 queries, 272,711.7 TPS, 294.49 interactivity, 75.67 kW
    • GB300: run 1, 16 queries, 3,054.0 TPS, 288.65 interactivity, 7.50 kW
  • Qwen3.6‑35B‑A3B
    • Vera Rubin: run 8, 320 queries, 47,785.5 TPS, 411.9 interactivity, 12.61 kW
    • GB300: run 2, 36 queries, 5,960.4 TPS, 531.6 interactivity, 7.50 kW

📈 Tradeoff Curve

  • Figure 2 shows the tradeoff between throughput per provisioned kilowatt and E2E interactivity across at least seven concurrency levels per curve.
  • The curves illustrate how much throughput each system delivers at a given responsiveness requirement.

🔬 Verification Status

  • GB300 results are verified by the MLCommons Association.
  • Vera Rubin results are provisional.
  • Pending MLCommons Association verification, results may change.

#MLPerf #NVIDIA #Inference #AgenticWorkloads #Throughput

Source: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Leads Agentic Inference Performance on MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: FlashOffloading Boosts LLM Serving Throughput by Offloading KV Cache to Host DRAM
item.description:
FlashOffloading Boosts LLM Serving Throughput by Offloading KV Cache to Host DRAM

FlashOffloading is a new host‑DRAM‑centric inference architecture that fully offloads the key‑value (KV) cache in large language model (LLM) serving, delivering higher throughput while meeting a 30 ms time‑per‑output‑token (TPOT) service‑level objective.

🔍 Overview

  • In LLM serving systems the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, quickly exhausting high‑bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity and limiting concurrency.
  • Moving the KV cache to host DRAM frees HBM space and allows higher concurrency, but the added cache management and host‑to‑device (H2D) load overhead increase inference latency, so the concurrency gain does not translate into effective throughput.

🧩 How it works

  • Rolling HBM cache for prefill – keeps a small active portion of the KV cache in HBM during the prefill phase.
  • Hot cache for decode – stores frequently accessed KV entries in host DRAM for decode.
  • Reverse sparse index – provides zero‑extra miss‑lookup overhead when locating KV entries.
  • Compute‑load overlapped kernel – overlaps computation with H2D data movement to reduce offloading latency across the entire pipeline.

⚙️ Performance gains

  • Deployed with GLM‑5.2 using multi‑token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill‑decode disaggregated platform.
  • Prefill throughput improves by up to 1.38×.
  • Decode throughput improves by up to 1.91×.
  • Gains are achieved while staying within a 30 ms TPOT constraint.

🚀 Availability

  • FlashOffloading has been integrated into an open‑source serving framework. See the implementation at this https URL.

#LLM #Inference #KVCache #DRAM

Source: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving

item.title: Microsoft launches Maia 300, third‑generation in‑house AI inference chip
item.description:
Microsoft launches Maia 300, third‑generation in‑house AI inference chip

Microsoft announced its third‑generation Maia 300 AI chip today, positioning it as the primary AI inference system for the company’s products and services.

🔍 Overview

  • Maia 300 is designed to improve the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud.
  • It is built to handle the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks.
  • The chip reduces Microsoft’s reliance on Nvidia GPUs and AMD solutions.
  • Production roll‑out is planned for 2027, with multi‑gigawatt Azure deployments beginning the same year.

🧩 How it works

  • Microsoft uses a chiplet architecture to gain efficiency gains.
  • The chip is fabricated on TSMC’s N2P process node.
  • Maia 300 separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions into distinct chiplets, which “increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” said the Azure hardware and infrastructure team.

⚙️ Key details

  • Performance: “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU‑based systems,” said Scott Guthrie, EVP of Microsoft’s cloud group.

item.title: Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
item.description:
Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers

This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the multi‑node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers. The deployment separates the prefill and decode phases onto distinct GPU workers behind a single OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.

🔍 Overview

  • Ray is a distributed compute framework; Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes.
  • AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) are pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately.
  • The new Ray LLM DLC extends this approach to multi‑node inference.

🏗️ Architecture

  • CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) runs system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod (CPU‑only).
  • Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run Ray workers: one dedicated to the prefill phase, the other to the decode phase.
  • Both GPU nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).
  • KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and automatically wires the head‑to‑worker join.
  • Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers.
  • KV‑cache generated by prefill is transferred to the decode worker over NIXL, using the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) through NIXL’s libfabric backend.

⚙️ How It Works

  • Prefill phase
    • Processes the entire input prompt in parallel.
    • Builds the key‑value (KV) cache.
    • Compute‑bound.
  • Decode phase
    • Generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending the KV cache.
    • Memory‑bandwidth‑bound.
  • Separating the phases prevents compute‑heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress.
  • Disaggregation allows each phase to use hardware and serving properties tuned to its workload, improving overall performance at scale.
  • The trade‑off is that the KV cache must be handed from prefill to decode quickly enough to retain the benefit.

📦 Key Components

Component Role
Ray LLM DLC Packages Ray Serve LLM, NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL), and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack; exposes an OpenAI‑compatible API with no application code
vLLM Inference engine
Ray Serve HTTP Serving layer
NIXL KV‑cache transfer between nodes
EFA stack (libfabric, aws‑ofi‑nccl) High‑bandwidth node‑to‑node communication
AWS Deep Learning Containers Pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images ensuring no version drift between CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer

🚀 Deployment Details

  • The Ray LLM DLC ships Ray Serve LLM, NIXL, and the EFA stack, ready for multi‑node inference.
  • No application code is required to expose the OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.
  • This multi‑node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as for prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads.
  • In a previous post, the Ray Serve DLC was used to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By assigning prefill and decode to separate GPUs, compute‑heavy prefill work no longer contends with latency‑sensitive decode work.
  • Independent scaling of each phase enables better resource utilization and lower latency for LLM serving at scale.
  • All components are validated together before each release, guaranteeing compatibility across the CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer.

#AWS #Ray #LLM #Kubernetes #Inference

Source: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI Updates Inference Capabilities and OpenAI Compatibility
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI Updates Inference Capabilities and OpenAI Compatibility

Amazon SageMaker AI has introduced new capabilities for deploying and consuming AI models, offering users paths for managed infrastructure or Kubernetes-native control with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference. In 2026, the platform delivered 13 new features to improve model deployment and optimization.

🔍 Overview

SageMaker AI now supports two primary deployment paths:

  • Managed endpoints: AWS handles infrastructure, operations, GPU provisioning, scaling, and monitoring.
  • Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference: Provides Kubernetes-native control for dedicated GPU clusters.

🧩 How it works

Inference recommendations automate the process of optimizing models based on performance goals such as cost, latency, or throughput. The system performs a three-step process:

  • Narrow: Filters instance types by analyzing model architecture and requirements.
  • Optimize: Applies techniques such as EAGLE 3.0 speculative decoding, kernel tuning, and tensor parallelism.
  • Benchmark: Runs NVIDIA AIPerf on real GPU infrastructure with multi-run confidence reporting.

⚙️ Key details

SageMaker now exposes an /openai/v1 path supporting Chat Completions with streaming, allowing for migration by simply updating the endpoint URL. Other technical improvements include:

  • Heterogeneous fleets: Customers can prioritize up to five instance types, with SageMaker automatically handling fallback and scaling based on capacity.
  • Optimized configurations: Each pool entry can reference unique configurations like quantization or speculative decoding generated by inference recommendations.
  • Metrics: Output includes validated metrics such as time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and throughput.

🚀 Availability

These features are supported for single-model, inference component, and async endpoints in all commercial AWS Regions. There is no additional cost for generating recommendations, and customers with ML Reservations can benchmark on reserved capacity at no extra charge.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker Inference Introduces Prefix-Aware Routing
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker Inference Introduces Prefix-Aware Routing

Amazon SageMaker Inference has introduced prefix-aware routing, a new routing strategy designed to optimize how requests are handled by instances.

🧩 How it works

Prefix-aware routing analyzes the beginning of each request payload to determine which instance should handle it. Its primary functions include:

  • Consistency: Requests with the same beginning are consistently sent to the same instance.
  • Distribution: Different beginnings are spread across different instances.
  • Cache Optimization: If multiple requests share a prefix, they are routed to the same machine to keep that machine’s cache warm.
  • Automated Management: The endpoint handles routing based on request content; users do not need to manage affinity or tag requests.
  • Load Balancing: If a target instance is at capacity due to a popular prefix, the endpoint routes the request to a less busy instance.
  • Stability: Most requests continue going to the same instance when instances are added or removed.

⚙️ Key details

Amazon SageMaker Inference now offers three routing strategies for real-time endpoints:

Strategy Description
RANDOM The default routing strategy.
LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS Routes based on outstanding requests.
PREFIX_AWARE New strategy that routes based on the request beginning.

Users can set the strategy per production variant in the endpoint configuration and switch between strategies without redeploying the model.

💡 Why it matters

In benchmarks using Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on 7 ml.p5.48xlarge instances with vLLM (prefix caching enabled), prefix-aware routing showed the following results compared to the random routing baseline:

General Impact

  • P50 TTFT reduced by up to 77 percent.
  • Throughput increased by up to 16 percent.
  • KV cache hit rates increased from roughly 25 percent to over 80 percent.

Specific Test Scenarios

  • 8,000-token shared prefixes (sustained over 1 hour):
    • P50 TTFT: Reduced by 71–77 percent.
    • P90 TTFT: Reduced by 33–37 percent.
    • Throughput: Increased 15–16 percent.
    • KV cache hit rate: Increased from approximately 25 to 82 percent.
  • Variable-length ShareGPT-style conversations (30 minutes):
    • P50 TTFT: Reduced by 13–16 percent.
    • P90 TTFT: Reduced by 24–37 percent.
    • Throughput: Increased 1.7–2.0 percent.
    • KV cache hit rate: Increased from approximately 30 to 80 percent.

Performance Overhead

  • The routing logic adds 1.3–1.9 milliseconds per request, while model TTFT in tests ranged from 63–280 milliseconds.
  • Traffic distribution remained balanced, with each of the 7 instances receiving 13.3–15.4 percent of requests.

#AmazonSageMaker #LLM #Inference #MachineLearning

Source: Reduce LLM latency with prefix-aware routing on Amazon SageMaker Inference | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA NIM Optimizes Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B Performance on Blackwell GPUs
item.description:
NVIDIA NIM Optimizes Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B Performance on Blackwell GPUs

NVIDIA NIM provides model- and GPU-aware serving choices packaged into a deployable microservice, offering validated performance engineering alongside an enterprise-ready container lifecycle.

🔍 Overview

NIM allows for the deployment of models like nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b. For production environments, NIM Certified provides commercial support through NVIDIA AI Enterprise, CVE handling, regular inference-stack updates, and broader hardware validation.

🧩 How it works

The optimized NIM stack employs several technical strategies to improve efficiency:

  • Hardware Mapping: Autotuned Mamba and mixture-of-experts kernels map hybrid architectures to NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs.
  • Parallelism: Tensor parallelism distributes the model across four GPUs, while expert-aware execution improves utilization for mixture-of-experts layers.
  • Memory and Cache: Prefix caching prevents the recomputation of repeated context, while partial-prefix matching recovers reuse when only part of a prefix matches. Mamba state-cache settings are tuned for the model architecture.
  • Workload Management: The system uses batched-token limits, concurrent-sequence limits, GPU-memory allocation, and block size to maintain work in flight without exceeding latency targets.
  • Decoding: The stack utilizes MTP speculative decoding and associated fixes.

⚙️ Key details

Performance benchmarks for agentic workloads (64K/400/76% KV reuse/50 TPS/user with 20 ms ITL) on 4xB200 hardware are as follows:

Configuration Throughput Notes
NIM Off baseline 718 tok/s No NIM optimizations
NIM On (2.0.12) 1,997 tok/s 2.5x v. Baseline

🚀 Availability

Users can deploy this via the Nemotron 3 Ultra NIM page by accepting governing terms and selecting the NIM 2.0.12 tag or published digest. Implementation details include:

  • Tag: export NIM_TAG=2.0.12
  • Image: nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:$NIM_TAG
  • Optimized Profile: For agentic workloads on a four-GPU B200 system, use vllm-nvidia-b200-nvfp4-tp4-pp1-throughput-90.0 and enable speculative decoding.
  • Benchmarking: NVIDIA AIPerf can be used to replay representative traffic, utilizing Mooncake-format JSONL traces or captured NIM requests.

#NVIDIA #NIM #Blackwell #LLM #Inference

item.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Supports Encode-Prefill-Decode Disaggregation for Multimodal Model Inference
item.description:
NVIDIA Dynamo Supports Encode-Prefill-Decode Disaggregation for Multimodal Model Inference

NVIDIA Dynamo, an open source inference framework for distributed environments, now supports Encode-Prefill-Decode (EPD) disaggregation. This optimization technique improves multimodal model performance by separating the vision encoder stage from the prefill and decode stages.

🧩 How it works

Dynamo implements EPD serving by separating encoder and PD (prefill-decode) worker roles. Instead of running these phases with tightly coupled scheduling, they are treated as independently scalable stages:

  • Encoder Workers: Produce vision embeddings.
  • PD Workers: Consume those embeddings and run the LLM.
  • Data Transfer: The NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL) is used to pass embeddings from encoder workers to PD workers.

⚙️ Key details

There are three primary placement options for these workers:

Placement Option Description
Aggregated Each GPU runs a single worker managing encoding, prefill, and decode for the entire request lifecycle.
Colocated Encoder Each GPU runs one or more encoder workers alongside one PD worker; generally the better fit for homogeneous clusters.
Disaggregated Encoder Encoder workers are placed on a lower-cost GPU tier while the primary GPU tier hosts PD workers.

In a test environment, two NVIDIA RTX 6000D GPUs were used for encoder workers, while four NVIDIA GB200 GPUs handled the PD workers. This configuration reserves the GB200 GPUs for the more memory- and compute-intensive LLM workload.

💡 Why it matters

EPD disaggregation isolates encoder work, which allows text requests to skip waiting for the encoder. This leads to improvements in batching, memory efficiency, and overall throughput.

Performance gains include:

  • Up to 5x faster time to first token (TTFT).
  • Up to 7x faster end-to-end response time.

The technique is most effective under the following conditions:

  • Image-heavy prompts.
  • Short-to-medium outputs.
  • Quantized mixture-of-experts (MoE) and lower-precision models (e.g., Qwen3.5 122B A10B NVFP4).
  • Scenarios where vision encoding accounts for a significant share of processing time or limits throughput.

Large dense models see less gain from this optimization.

#NVIDIA #Dynamo #LLM #MultimodalAI #Inference

Source: When to Use Encode-Prefill-Decode Disaggregation to Accelerate Multimodal Model Serving | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Recent Developments in LLM KV Cache Compression and Efficiency
item.description:
Recent Developments in LLM KV Cache Compression and Efficiency

New research introduces two distinct approaches to optimizing key-value (KV) cache memory usage in large language models to address bottlenecks in long-context inference and reasoning workloads.

🔍 Overview

KV cache growth poses a significant memory bottleneck for LLM serving. Two new frameworks, GrowPage and SGD-KV, provide methods to manage cache memory more efficiently.

🧩 How it works

Framework Methodology Primary Focus
GrowPage On-demand budgeting Dynamically adjusts KV capacity based on runtime demand variations.
SGD-KV Summarization-Guided Compression Uses a head-aware diagnostic task to prioritize attention heads.

⚙️ Key details

GrowPage

  • Treats KV capacity as a runtime resource that evolves during generation.
  • Maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to estimate demand.
  • Integrates with PagedAttention to preserve continuous batching and prefix caching.
  • Adjusts capacity by compressing states or acquiring additional physical pages as needed.

SGD-KV

  • Employs a chunk-summarization diagnostic task to identify heads specialized in hierarchical information aggregation.
  • Reduces KV cache memory usage by up to 75%.
  • Maintains performance on benchmarks up to 1M context tokens.
  • Tested on Qwen2.5-7B-1M and Qwen3-32B models.

💡 Why it matters

Both methods offer improved performance-to-throughput or efficiency-to-accuracy trade-offs, enabling more effective long-context inference and reasoning.

#LLM #KVCache #AI #MachineLearning #Inference

Source: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving Source: SGD-KV: Summarization Guided KV Cache Compression

item.title: Nvidia Introduces Integrated Rubin‑Vera System for End‑to‑End Agent Workloads
item.description:
Nvidia Introduces Integrated Rubin‑Vera System for End‑to‑End Agent Workloads

Nvidia is expanding its focus from raw GPU horsepower to full‑stack hardware that can run agentic workloads from start to finish. By pairing Rubin GPUs with a Vera CPU and additional supporting units, the company aims to cut data movement and speed up the orchestration needed for multi‑step AI agents.

🛠️ Hardware Architecture

  • Rubin GPUs + Vera CPU – The combination is designed to keep data close to compute, reducing latency caused by moving information between separate components.
  • Supporting units – Additional hardware is included to further accelerate orchestration of complex, multi‑step agents.

⚡ Performance Highlights

  • Vera’s orchestration role is reported to deliver up to 3× improvements on certain I/O‑heavy operations.
  • The design shifts emphasis from GPU throughput alone to overall latency, memory orchestration, and data plumbing.

📦 Deployment Implications

  • Integrated racks that bundle CPU, GPU, flash storage, and accelerators are expected from hardware partners and cloud vendors.
  • This changes procurement and cost‑modeling decisions, as well as considerations about where sensitive workflows are deployed.

📈 Guidance for Founders and Operators

  • Stop treating the GPU as the whole stack; evaluate full‑stack latency and token cost (model inference plus orchestration overhead) against end‑to‑end hardware profiles.
  • When negotiating with cloud providers, request agent‑focused SLAs and detailed specifications of memory and access patterns before committing to large‑scale deployments.

✅ Key Takeaways

  • Agent performance now hinges on the entire hardware stack, not just GPU speed.
  • Nvidia’s Rubin‑Vera pairing promises notable I/O gains, potentially lowering the cost of running production agents.
  • Organizations should benchmark complete end‑to‑end latency and seek contracts that reflect the broader resource needs of agentic workloads.

#Nvidia #AIagents #Hardware #Inference #Deployment
